justification: Congenital reticular ichthyosiform erythroderma (ichthyosis with confetti) is well established to be caused by frameshift/mutant keratin alleles in KRT10 and, less commonly, KRT1, with revertant mosaicism via mitotic recombination explaining the confetti-like normal skin spots. MC2R encodes the ACTH receptor and its variants cause familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 1, a disorder of adrenal steroidogenesis with hyperpigmentation, not a keratinization disorder. There is no reported human genetic evidence, functional data, or animal model linking MC2R to CRIE; melanocortin receptor biology in skin (mainly MC1R) provides only a tenuous, indirect conceptual link. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for speculative pigment/melanocortin-pathway hypotheses.

HPS1 variants are well established as causing Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome type 1, characterized by oculocutaneous albinism, platelet storage pool deficiency with bleeding diathesis, granulomatous colitis, and progressive pulmonary fibrosis — not a skeletal muscle disorder. Myosclerosis (myosclerosis myopathy) is a recognized entity attributable to COL6A2 (collagen VI–related myopathy) variants, with no reported HPS1 involvement in human probands or families. The only tenuous conceptual link is the fibrotic phenotype (pulmonary fibrosis in HPS) and lysosome-related organelle/trafficking biology, which could hypothetically be invoked for tissue fibrosis, but there is no muscle-specific expression, model, or pathway evidence connecting HPS1 to myosclerosis. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for a speculative fibrosis-based hypothesized link.

PTS encodes 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase, and its biallelic variants cause tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency with hyperphenylalaninemia and neurotransmitter deficits, a phenotype entirely distinct from organic aciduria. 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaric aciduria is caused by deficiency of HMG-CoA lyase (HMGCL), with related leucine/ketogenesis pathway defects (e.g., AUH, HMGCS2) accounting for phenocopies. There is no known biochemical or pathway link between pterin biosynthesis and leucine catabolism/ketogenesis that would produce elevated 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate. Any co-mention of PTS and HMG-CoA lyase deficiency would arise incidentally from newborn screening or metabolic panel literature rather than from causal evidence. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only small residual probability for speculative or incidental reports.

3M syndrome 2 is a well-defined autosomal recessive primordial growth disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in OBSL1 (with 3M1 caused by CUL7 and 3M3 by CCDC8); ADCY5 is not part of this CUL7–OBSL1–CCDC8 complex or its recognized disease spectrum. ADCY5 variants in humans cause ADCY5-related dyskinesia (familial dyskinesia with facial myokymia) and common variants are associated with birth weight, fetal growth, and type 2 diabetes. The birth-weight/fetal-growth GWAS association provides only a tenuous, nonspecific biological rationale for a growth-restriction phenotype, which could support a weak "hypothesized" reading but not a link to 3M syndrome 2 specifically. There are no reported ADCY5 variants in 3M syndrome patients or families, so the relationship is essentially novel/incidental.

Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia 83 (SPG83, MIM 619027) is caused by biallelic variants in HPDL, encoding a mitochondrial 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase-like protein, with multiple independent families reported. LEPR encodes the leptin receptor and its established human disease association is autosomal recessive obesity with hypogonadism and hyperphagia, not hereditary spastic paraplegia. I am not aware of any human genetic study, functional study, or animal model linking LEPR variants or leptin signaling to SPG83 or to a comparable corticospinal degeneration phenotype. A small residual probability is retained for speculative neurobiological arguments (leptin signaling in neuronal survival/metabolism) that could be framed as hypothesized, but there is no direct or indirect evidence for this specific gene–phenotype pair.

DBT encodes the E2 dihydrolipoamide branched-chain transacylase subunit of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, and biallelic variants are well established as a cause of maple syrup urine disease type II, a metabolic disorder unrelated to protein aggregate myopathies. Myofibrillar myopathy 5 (MFM5) is specifically attributed to variants in FLNC (filamin C), with other MFM subtypes caused by DES, CRYAB, MYOT, LDB3, BAG3, and others; DBT is not among these. No credible human genetic studies report DBT variants in myofibrillar myopathy patients, and there is no compelling mechanistic link between branched-chain amino acid catabolism and sarcomeric/Z-disc protein aggregation. A small residual probability is retained for hypothesized status because metabolic dysfunction can secondarily affect skeletal muscle, and MSUD patients can show nonspecific myopathic features, but this does not constitute evidence for MFM5.

SBDS is the well-established cause of Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, bone marrow failure, skeletal dysplasia, and variable immune defects), whereas IPEX syndrome is caused by FOXP3 mutations, with IPEX-like phenotypes attributed to genes such as IL2RA, STAT5B, STAT1, LRBA, CTLA4, ITCH, and DOCK8. There are no reported human genetic studies implicating SBDS variants in IPEX or IPEX-like disease. Some conceptual overlap exists because SDS features malabsorption/enteropathy-like symptoms, immune dysfunction (B- and T-cell abnormalities, hypogammaglobulinemia), and pancreatic endocrine/exocrine involvement, so SBDS could occasionally appear in a differential diagnosis or in ribosomopathy-immune dysregulation discussions, giving modest weight to "Hypothesized." Overall, evidence for a causal or associative link with IPEX specifically is essentially absent, so the relationship is best considered novel with limited biological plausibility.

phenotype: blepharophimosis - intellectual disability syndrome, MKB type
justification: LPAR6 (P2RY5), located within an intron of RB1, is well established as the gene for autosomal recessive hypotrichosis simplex/woolly hair (hypotrichosis 8), with no known role in neurodevelopmental or craniofacial syndromes. Blepharophimosis–intellectual disability syndrome, Maat-Kievit-Brunner (MKB) type, is an X-linked Ohdo-like syndrome attributed to SMARCA1 variants, while the related SBBYSS form is caused by KAT6B. There is no reported human genetic evidence, functional overlap, or plausible shared pathway (LPAR6 encodes a lysophosphatidic acid GPCR acting in hair follicle differentiation) linking LPAR6 to this phenotype. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental, so the relationship is best classified as novel, with a small allowance for speculative biological/pathway-based hypotheses.

Surfactant metabolism dysfunction, pulmonary, 4 (SMDP4) is a hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by biallelic CSF2RA (with related forms from CSF2RB, SFTPB, SFTPC, ABCA3) defects, and FGF3 has no reported role in GM-CSF receptor signaling or surfactant catabolism. FGF3 variants in humans are established causes of LAMM syndrome (congenital deafness with labyrinthine aplasia, microtia, microdontia) and FGF3 is implicated in 11q13 amplification in cancer, not in neonatal/childhood interstitial lung disease. Some FGF family members (notably FGF10/FGFR2b) are central to branching morphogenesis and alveolar type II cell differentiation, providing a weak, indirect biological rationale that could support a "hypothesized" link, but FGF3 itself is not a recognized lung developmental regulator. No human genetic or clinical study links FGF3 variants to surfactant dysfunction, so the association is best considered novel with a small allowance for pathway-level speculation.

phenotype: polymicrogyria, perisylvian, with cerebellar hypoplasia and arthrogryposis
justification: Polymicrogyria, perisylvian, with cerebellar hypoplasia and arthrogryposis (PMGYCHA, OMIM 616531) is a recessive disorder attributed to biallelic variants in PI4KA, with related phenotypes linked to genes in phosphoinositide and tubulin pathways; PDCD1 is not among the reported causal genes. PDCD1 encodes the immune checkpoint receptor PD-1, whose human genetic associations concern autoimmunity (e.g., SLE, type 1 diabetes), immunodeficiency with autoimmune/inflammatory disease, and tumor immunology, not cortical malformations. There is no known mechanistic or pathway connection between PD-1 signaling and perisylvian polymicrogyria, cerebellar hypoplasia, or arthrogryposis, and no reported animal models linking Pdcd1 loss to these brain malformations. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental (e.g., large sequencing panels or unrelated immunology contexts). Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a small allowance for speculative neuroimmune/neurodevelopmental biology arguments.

SMAD2 is an autosomal gene at 18q21.1, whereas intellectual disability, X-linked 96 is by definition caused by a locus on the X chromosome, making a direct causal relationship implausible. Human SMAD2 variants are established in a connective tissue/arterial aneurysm and complex congenital heart disease phenotype (Loeys-Dietz-like spectrum), sometimes with variable developmental delay, but not in any X-linked ID entity. Any conceivable link is indirect and biological, via TGF-beta/activin-SMAD signaling in neurodevelopment and cortical progenitor regulation, largely from animal and in vitro work. Therefore the vast majority of weight belongs to Novel, with a small allowance for pathway-based Hypothesized reasoning and minimal weight for Existing/Established.

Knobloch syndrome type 1 is caused by biallelic COL18A1 variants, and Knobloch syndrome 2 (OMIM 608454) was mapped to chromosome 17q11.2 in a single consanguineous family with the causative gene still unidentified; ADAMTS18 has also been proposed for Knobloch-like phenotypes. PAX9 maps to 14q13.3, outside the KNO2 linkage interval, and its established human disease association is with tooth agenesis/oligodontia (and modifier effects in orofacial clefting), not with occipital encephalocele or vitreoretinal degeneration. I am not aware of any human genetic study implicating PAX9 variants in Knobloch syndrome 2. A small amount of probability is retained for "Hypothesized" because PAX9 is a developmental transcription factor with craniofacial/palatal roles in knockout mice, offering a very loose biological rationale for neural-tube/craniofacial malformation, but this is speculative and not phenotype-specific.

Ritscher-Schinzel (3C, cranio-cerebello-cardiac) syndrome has well-defined molecular causes: biallelic WASHC5/KIAA0196 (RTSC1), X-linked CCDC22 (RTSC2), and VPS35L (RTSC3), all converging on the WASH/CCC-retriever endosomal trafficking machinery. SFRP4 is a secreted Wnt antagonist whose human disease association is Pyle metaphyseal dysplasia, not Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome, and I am aware of no probands or families with SFRP4 variants presenting the 3C phenotype. A weak indirect biological rationale exists because CCC/retriever components modulate Wnt receptor recycling and Wnt signaling is critical for cerebellar vermis and cardiac outflow development, which could support a "hypothesized" pathway-level connection. However, this is speculative and not supported by any reported human genetic evidence, so the majority of probability falls on "Novel," with a modest allocation to "Hypothesized."

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis type 9 (ALS9) is a well-defined Mendelian entity attributed to mutations in ANG (angiogenin) on chromosome 14q11.2, with no recognized role for ADAM20 in its OMIM/ClinGen curation. ADAM20 is a predominantly testis-expressed disintegrin/metalloprotease with no established neuronal or motor-neuron function, and I am unaware of any human genetic study reporting ADAM20 variants segregating with or associated with ALS9 specifically. At most, ADAM20 could be co-mentioned incidentally in exome/GWAS variant lists or in generic discussions of the ADAM metalloprotease family (where ADAM10/ADAM17 have neurodegeneration relevance), which would support only a weak hypothesized link by family analogy. Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly favors "Novel," with a modest allowance for hypothesized pathway/family-based speculation and a small residual chance that an unreplicated human sequencing report exists.

Microphthalmia, isolated, with coloboma 6 (MCOPCB6, OMIM 613703) is attributed in the literature to GDF3 variants, not IL17RD. IL17RD (SEF) is best known in human genetics as a cause/modifier of normosmic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and Kallmann syndrome, acting as a negative regulator of FGF receptor signaling. Because FGF signaling is central to optic vesicle/optic fissure development and FGFR1 pathway defects can produce ocular anomalies including coloboma, a biologically plausible (hypothesized) link exists, and some HH patient series mention variable ocular findings. However, I am not aware of any human genetic study reporting IL17RD variants in isolated microphthalmia with coloboma, so the evidence falls mainly between "novel" and "hypothesized."

The Orphanet entity "short stature–brachydactyly–obesity–global developmental delay syndrome" (SBIDDS) is classically attributed to biallelic PRMT7 variants, not to ATP5F1A. ATP5F1A (ATP synthase F1 alpha subunit) is established as a cause of mitochondrial complex V deficiency/combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, presenting with neonatal encephalopathy, hypotonia, lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy, and more recently with neurodegenerative/spastic phenotypes — none of which include the brachydactyly–obesity constellation. The only conceivable overlap is nonspecific global developmental delay and growth failure seen in mitochondrial disease, which provides a weak biological rationale but no phenotype-specific genetic evidence. I therefore weight Novel most heavily, with some allowance for Hypothesized based on shared nonspecific neurodevelopmental features, and only small probability that an individual human case report links ATP5F1A to this specific syndrome.

SLK (STE20-like kinase, 10q25.1) is not among the recognized Mendelian high-myopia genes (e.g., ZNF644, SCO2, LRPAP1, CTSH, SLC39A5, ARR3, P4HA2), so an "Established" causal role in degenerative/pathologic myopia is very unlikely. However, large refractive-error/myopia GWAS meta-analyses (CREAM, 23andMe, UK Biobank; Tedja 2018, Hysi 2020) implicate hundreds of loci and many kinase/cytoskeletal genes, so it is plausible that SLK has been reported as a candidate at a refractive-error locus, which would qualify as "Existing" since refractive error/high myopia is a direct precursor of degenerative myopia. Biologically, SLK regulates cytoskeletal remodeling, cell migration, and apoptosis—processes relevant to scleral remodeling and retinal/RPE integrity—supporting a "Hypothesized" link even without variant data, though such reasoning is generic. Absent any specific recollection of SLK in myopia literature, a substantial probability remains that mentions are incidental and the pair is effectively novel.

The designated gene for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 16 (CMH16, OMIM 613838) is MYOZ2, not MYO18B, so MYO18B is not the established cause of this specific subtype. MYO18B's confirmed human disease association is autosomal recessive nemaline myopathy 30 / Klippel-Feil anomaly-myopathy-cardiac defects syndrome, in which some patients show cardiac involvement (septal defects, occasional cardiomyopathy), giving limited but non-zero human evidence for a cardiac phenotype rather than classic HCM. Strong supporting biology exists: MYO18B is essential for sarcomere assembly and myofibrillar integrity, and Myo18b-null mice and zebrafish mutants show severe cardiac and skeletal muscle sarcomere disorganization, which supports a "Hypothesized" mechanistic link. Occasional appearance of MYO18B as a candidate/rare variant in cardiomyopathy sequencing panels provides weak, unreplicated human data. Therefore most weight falls on Hypothesized, with meaningful probability for Existing and Novel and minimal support for Established.

Hereditary renal hypouricemia is a well-defined Mendelian disorder caused almost exclusively by loss-of-function variants in SLC22A12 (URAT1, RHUC type 1) and SLC2A9 (GLUT9, RHUC type 2), with rare unexplained cases attributed to as-yet-unidentified transporters; IDH2 has never been reported as a causal gene, so "Established" is essentially excluded. IDH2 is primarily known for germline variants causing D-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria type II and somatic variants in myeloid malignancies and gliomas, none of which involve renal urate handling. There is some possibility that the IDH2/UBE2Q2 region on 15q26 has appeared among common-variant loci in large serum urate GWAS, which would support a modest "Existing" weight since serum urate level is the quantitative trait underlying hypouricemia, but I am not confident this locus is genuinely IDH2-attributed. A "Hypothesized" role could be argued from metabolic/mitochondrial contributions to proximal tubule energetics and 2-hydroxyglutarate effects on transport, but such biology is indirect and not specifically tied to urate excretion. Overall, the most likely classification is Novel, with meaningful residual probability spread across Existing and Hypothesized.

SMC3 is best known as a cohesin complex subunit whose mutations cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome 3, and its core biology (chromosome cohesion, transcriptional regulation) has no obvious direct link to airway inflammation. However, the phenotype label "Asthma-related traits, susceptibility to, 5" is a specific OMIM designation that is typically assigned only when at least one human genetic association/linkage study implicates the gene (SMC3 lies at 10q25, a region reported in asthma/atopy linkage and candidate-gene work), which fits the "Existing" tier of limited, non-definitive human evidence. Such susceptibility designations are rarely supported by replicated causal proband/family data, so "Established" is very unlikely. A modest probability is retained for "Novel"/"Hypothesized" in case the pairing reflects only an incidental or purely biological/expression-based co-mention rather than a genuine human association study.
